frames.narration: A match ends. The game server, not the phone, computes the player's score and sends it to the score API with a server credential and the match id. The API checks that the score is plausible for one match.
The player's id hashes to shard 3. The API updates the player in that shard's sorted set, in the daily, weekly and all-time boards. It takes microseconds.
The same update goes on the queue, and a writer saves it in the scores database, which is the durable source of truth. If the match id was seen before, the writer ignores the repeat.
The player opens the leaderboard and asks for the top 100. The API asks every shard for its own top 100 in parallel.

Each shard answers from memory. Anyone in the global top 100 is certainly in the top 100 of their own shard, so merging the lists gives exactly the right answer. The merged list is cached for one second.
The player also wants their own rank. The API asks every shard one cheap question: how many players have a better score than 2,450? Each shard answers by searching its sorted set.
The counts are added up: 18,204 players are better, so the rank is 18,205. The same search gives the players just above and below, so the app can show the neighbours.

A little later this player overtakes the one above. The shard publishes the change, and the push gateway sends one batched message to the phones that are watching this part of the board, so nobody has to refresh.
